\section[a inveja]{a inveja — envy}

\label{lesson:PT-C468-inveja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to be proud, then the Portuguese for to boast.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a inveja}
\textbf{a inveja} — \textquotedblleft{}envy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tenho inveja das tuas férias na praia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I envy you your holiday at the beach.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ter inveja de} — to envy. \emph{O ciúme} is jealousy in love.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{inveja} is inherited from Latin \emph{invidia} \textquotedblleft{}envy, ill will\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{invidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to look askance at, to begrudge\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a inveja}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a inveja}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a inveja}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to be proud, then the Portuguese for to boast, then say \emph{a inveja} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a inveja mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Envy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[invejoso]{invejoso — envious}

\label{lesson:PT-C468-invejoso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to boast, then the Portuguese for envy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: invejoso}
\textbf{invejoso} — \textquotedblleft{}envious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O vizinho invejoso não gosta do nosso carro novo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The envious neighbour does not like our new car.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{a inveja} with \emph{-oso}; a woman is \emph{invejosa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{invejoso} is built on \emph{inveja} \textquotedblleft{}envy\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{invidia} (Lewis \& Short); compare Latin \emph{invidiōsus} \textquotedblleft{}envious\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to boast, then the Portuguese for envy, then say \emph{invejoso} again

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[invejar]{invejar — to envy}

\label{lesson:PT-C468-invejar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for envy, then the Portuguese for envious.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: invejar}
\textbf{invejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to envy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Invejo a calma da minha irmã.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I envy my sister's calm.}
\end{quote}

A little more formal than \emph{ter inveja de}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{invejar} is built on \emph{inveja} \textquotedblleft{}envy\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{invidia} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[egoísta]{egoísta — selfish; selfish person}

\label{lesson:PT-C468-egoista}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for envious, then the Portuguese for to envy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: egoísta}
\textbf{egoísta} — \textquotedblleft{}selfish; selfish person\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele é egoísta e nunca partilha nada.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is selfish and never shares anything.}
\end{quote}

The same form for a man and a woman: \emph{um egoísta}, \emph{uma egoísta}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{egoísta} was borrowed from French \emph{égoïste} (EtymDB), a modern word built on Latin \emph{ego} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{egoísta}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{egoísta}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{egoísta}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for envious, then the Portuguese for to envy, then say \emph{egoísta} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does egoísta mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Selfish; selfish person\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[o egoísmo]{o egoísmo — selfishness}

\label{lesson:PT-C468-egoismo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to envy, then the Portuguese for selfish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o egoísmo}
\textbf{o egoísmo} — \textquotedblleft{}selfishness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O egoísmo estraga muitas amizades.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Selfishness spoils many friendships.}
\end{quote}

The person is \emph{um egoísta}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{egoísmo} is usually traced to French \emph{égoïsme}, built like \emph{égoïste} on Latin \emph{ego} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB records that French source for \emph{egoísta} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
